claim: The Cam-CAN dataset is currently the largest public resource on multimodal imaging with high-resolution electrophysiology in the form of MEG alongside MRI data and rich neuropsychological data for more than 650 healthy subjects between 17 and 90 years.
source: The Cam-CAN dataset is currently the largest public resource on multimodal imaging with high-resolution electrophysiology in the form of MEG alongside MRI data and rich neuropsychological data for more than 650 healthy subjects between 17 and 90 years.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Cam-CAN dataset characteristics that is directly stated in the manuscript.

claim: MEG and EEG share the same classes of neural generators.
source: Fortunately, MEG and EEG share the same classes of neural generators, rendering the aging-related EEG-literature highly relevant for MEG-based modeling.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the relationship between MEG and EEG.

claim: MEG preferentially captures tangential but not radial sources compared to EEG.
source: While EEG captures sources of any orientation, MEG preferentially captures tangential but not radial sources.
evidence: This is a statement about the biophysical properties of MEG that is presented as established knowledge.

claim: MEG benefits from the magnetic transparency of the skull, which facilitates source localization.
source: Compared to EEG, MEG benefits from the magnetic transparency of the skull, which facilitates source localization by reducing the risk of errors due to an incorrect head conductivity model, but also by limiting the large-scale mixing of neural sources.
evidence: This statement describes a known biophysical advantage of MEG over EEG.

claim: MEG has significantly increased signal-to-noise ratio in higher frequencies compared to EEG.
source: This significantly increases the signal-to-noise ratio for MEG in higher frequencies, rendering it a formidable technique for studying cortical oscillatory activity (Lehtelä et al., 1997; Gobbelé et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The full multimodal model achieved the first rank 71 out of 100 times in cross-validation.
source: Moreover, the out-of-sample ranking between the different models was stable over cross-validation folds (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with the full model achieving the first rank 71/100 times and performing at least 80/100 better than the MRI + fMRI or the MRI + MEG model.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results with reference to a figure.

claim: Peak frequency and power drop in the alpha band (8–12 Hz) has been linked to aging-related slowing of cognitive processes.
source: Peak frequency and power drop in the alpha band (8–12 Hz), assessed by EEG, has been linked to aging-related slowing of cognitive processes, such as the putative speed of attention (Richard Clark et al., 2004; Babiloni et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased anteriorization of beta band power (15–30 Hz) has been associated with effortful compensatory mechanisms.
source: Increased anteriorization of beta band power (15–30 Hz) has been associated with effortful compensatory mechanisms (Gola et al., 2013) in response to intensified levels of neural noise, that is, decreased temporal autocorrelation of the EEG signal as revealed by flatter 1/f slopes (Voytek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Age-related variability in fMRI and EEG seems to be independent to a substantial degree.
source: Importantly, age-related variability in fMRI and EEG seems to be independent to a substantial degree (Kumral et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The study included 674 healthy individuals between 18 and 88 years with an average of 54.2 years.
source: Our sample comprised 674 (340 female) healthy individuals between 18 (female = 18) to 88 (female = 87) years with an average of 54.2 (female = 53.7) and a standard deviation of 18.7 (female = 18.8) years.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study sample.

claim: The most informative MEG features for age prediction were ridge regression models based on signal power or Hilbert analytic signal power concatenated across frequency bands.
source: The most informative input to the stacking model were ridge regression models based on either signal power or the Hilbert analytic signal power concatenated across frequency bands (Pcat, Ecat).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from variable importance analysis.

claim: Source power in the beta (15–30 Hz) and alpha (8–15 Hz) frequency bands made noteworthy contributions to age prediction.
source: Other noteworthy contributions were related to power envelope covariance (without source leakage correction) as well as source power in the beta (15–30 Hz) and alpha (8–15 Hz) band frequency range.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from variable importance analysis.

claim: Models based on source-level power spectra showed expected errors between 8 and 6.5 years.
source: All models featuring source-level power spectra or connectivity ('Source Activity, Source Connectivity') performed visibly better, with expected errors between 8 and 6.5 years and no overlap with the distribution of chance-level scores.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results.

claim: Brain age delta showed associations with about 20-25% of all neuropsychological measures included.
source: Traditional significance testing (Figure 3A) suggests that the best stacking models supported discoveries for between 20% (7) and 25% (9) of the scores.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Larger values of brain age delta were globally associated with elevated depression scores, higher blood pressure, lower sleep quality, lower fluid intelligence, lower scores in neurological assessment and lower memory performance.
source: In this sample, larger values of the Δ were globally associated with elevated depression scores, higher blood pressure, lower sleep quality, lower fluid intelligence, lower scores in neurological assessment and lower memory performance.
evidence: This is a summary of the brain-behavior correlation results from the study.

claim: The association with depression appeared first when predicting age from fMRI.
source: For example, the association with depression appeared first when predicting age from fMRI.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the brain-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: The association with fluid intelligence and sleep quality visibly intensified when including MEG.
source: Likewise, the association with fluid intelligence and sleep quality visibly intensified when including MEG.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the brain-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: Stacking allows to enhance brain-age prediction by extracting information from MEG, fMRI and MRI while mitigating modality-specific errors.
source: These findings demonstrate that stacking allows to enhance brain-age prediction by extracting information from MEG, fMRI and MRI while mitigating modality-specific errors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: MEG and fMRI both substantially improved age-prediction when combined with anatomical MRI.
source: Our results suggest that MEG and fMRI both substantially improved age-prediction when combined with anatomical MRI.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: MEG and fMRI convey non-redundant information on cognitive functioning and health.
source: Our results suggest that MEG and fMRI convey non-redundant information on cognitive functioning and health, for example fluid intelligence, memory, sleep quality, cognitive decline and depression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the brain-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: The opportunistic stacking model performed equivalently to the restricted model on common subsets of the data.
source: Our stacking model, trained on the entire data with an opportunistic strategy, performed equivalently to the restricted model on common subsets of the data and helped exploiting multimodal information to the extent available.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results comparing opportunistic and restricted models.

claim: MEG and fMRI helped gain almost 1 year of error compared to purely anatomy-based prediction.
source: Both, MEG and fMRI helped gain almost 1 year of error compared to purely anatomy-based prediction.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: The improvements of MEG and fMRI over anatomical MRI are due to their access to complementary information that helps predicting distinct cases.
source: This additional finding suggests that the improvements of MEG and fMRI over anatomical MRI are due to their access to complementary information that helps predicting distinct cases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the weak correlation between MEG and fMRI prediction errors.

claim: Connectivity features, in general, and power-envelope connectivity, in particular, contributed substantively to age prediction.
source: However, connectivity features, in general, and power-envelope connectivity, in particular, contributed substantively (Figure 4B, Table 4).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from variable importance analysis.

claim: Applying orthogonalization for removing source leakage did not notably improve performance.
source: Interestingly, applying orthogonalization (Hipp et al., 2012; Hipp and Siegel, 2015) for removing source leakage did not notably improve performance (Table 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results.

claim: The fMRI signal in elderly populations might predominantly reflect vascular effects rather than neuronal activity.
source: Recent findings based on the dataset analyzed in the present study have shown that the fMRI signal in elderly populations might predominantly reflect vascular effects rather than neuronal activity (Tsvetanov et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on the same dataset.

claim: The observed complementarity of fMRI and MEG in age prediction might be conservatively explained by the age-related increase in the ratio of vascular to neuronal contributions to the fMRI signal.
source: The observed complementarity of the fMRI and MEG in age prediction might, therefore, be conservatively explained by the age-related increase in the ratio of vascular to neuronal contributions to the fMRI signal, while MEG signals are directly induced by neuronal activity, regardless of aging.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results considering the vascular confound in fMRI.

claim: Electrophysiology can make a difference in prediction problems in which fast brain rhythms are strongly statistically related to the biomedical outcome of interest.
source: In sum, our findings suggest that electrophysiology can make a difference in prediction problems in which fast brain rhythms are strongly statistically related to the biomedical outcome of interest.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The brain age delta shows substantive associations with about 20–25% of all neuropsychological measures included.
source: Our findings suggest that the brain age Δ shows substantive associations with about 20–25% of all neuropsychological measures included.
evidence: This is a summary of the brain-behavior correlation results.

claim: The overall picture is congruent with the brain age literature and supports the interpretation of the brain age delta as index of decline of physical health, well-being and cognitive fitness.
source: The overall big-picture is congruent with the brain age literature (see discussion in Smith et al., 2019 for an overview) and supports the interpretation of the brain age Δ as index of decline of physical health, well-being and cognitive fitness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results in the context of previous literature.

claim: fMRI and MEG contributed additive, if not unique information to brain-behavior associations.
source: Most strikingly, we found that fMRI and MEG contributed additive, if not unique information (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the brain-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: Predicting biomedical outcomes from multiple modalities may reduce susceptibility to 'modality impurity'.
source: In this context, it is worwhile considering that predicting biomedical outcomes from multiple modalities may reduce susceptibility to 'modality impurity' as often observed in modeling of individual differences in cognitive abilities (Friedman and Miyake, 2004; Miyake et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with reference to previous literature on modality impurity.

claim: Cardiac measures were exclusively related to fMRI-based models and vanished as MEG was included.
source: In the present study, it was remarkable that cardiac measures were exclusively related to fMRI-based models and vanished as MEG was included.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the brain-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: The Cam-CAN sample consists of healthy individuals only.
source: Indeed, the strength of linear association was below 0.5 in units of standard deviations of the normalized predictors and the target. On the other hand, it is important to consider that the Cam-CAN sample consists of healthy individuals only.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study sample.

claim: Brain age delta might be used as a screening tool for a wide array of clinical settings.
source: This suggests that brain age Δ might be used as a screening tool for a wide array of clinical settings for which the Cam-CAN dataset could serve as a normative sample.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about potential clinical applications.

claim: Adding extra cases with incomplete measurements never harmed prediction of the cases with complete data.
source: In fact, adding extra cases with incomplete measurements never harmed prediction of the cases with complete data and the full multimodal stacking always outperformed sub-models with fewer modalities (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results on opportunistic learning.

claim: The opportunistic approach allowed maintaining and extending the performance to new cases with incomplete modalities.
source: Moreover, the approach allowed maintaining and extending the performance to new cases with incomplete modalities (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results on opportunistic learning.

claim: Source power can be approximated by the sensor-level topography of power spectra which can be computed on any multichannel EEG device.
source: This is because it suggests that a rather simple statistical object accounts for the bulk of the performance of MEG. Source power can be approximated by the sensor-level topography of power spectra which can be computed on any multichannel EEG device in a few steps and only yields as many variables per frequency band as there are channels.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical implications of the findings for EEG applications.

claim: Computing the power spectrum amounts to estimating the marginal expectation of the signal variance, which can be thought of as main effect.
source: Moreover, from a statistical standpoint, computing the power spectrum amounts to estimating the marginal expectation of the signal variance, which can be thought of as main effect.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical properties of power spectra.

claim: Connectivity is often operationalized as bivariate interaction, which gives rise to a more complex statistical object of higher dimensionality.
source: On the other hand, connectivity is often operationalized as bivariate interaction, which gives rise to a more complex statistical object of higher dimensionality whose precise, reproducible estimation may require far more samples.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical properties of connectivity measures.

claim: The findings may generalize and similar performance can be unlocked on simpler EEG devices with fewer channels.
source: This nourishes the hope that our findings will generalize and similar performance can be unlocked on simpler EEG devices with fewer channels.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential generalization to EEG.

claim: Source localization may be critical for resolving changes in the source geometry of the power spectrum.
source: While clinical EEG may not well resolve functional connectivity it may be good enough to resolve changes in the source geometry of the power spectrum (Sabbagh et al., 2020). On the other hand, source localization may be critical in this context as linear field spread actually results in a non-linear transform when considering the power of a source (Sabbagh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of source localization with references to previous work.

claim: The Cam-CAN is a unique resource of multimodal neuroimaging data with sufficient data points to enable machine learning approaches.
source: The Cam-CAN is a unique resource of multimodal neuroimaging data with sufficient data points to enable machine learning approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of the dataset used.

claim: From the point of view of machine learning, the Cam-CAN dataset is a small dataset.
source: Yet, from the point of view of machine learning, the Cam-CAN dataset is a small dataset.
evidence: This is an assessment of the dataset size in the context of machine learning.

claim: If the Cam-CAN included many more data points beyond 10-100k subjects, the proposed stacking model might possibly be of limited advantage compared to purely non-linear models.
source: If the Cam-CAN included many more data points, for example beyond 10–100 k subjects, the proposed stacking model might possibly be of limited advantage compared to purely non-linear models, for example random forests, gradient boosting or deep learning methods (Bzdok and Yeo, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations with larger datasets.

claim: The fact that the Cam-CAN has been unique so far hinders generalization testing to equivalent multimodal datasets from other sites.
source: At the same time, the fact that the Cam-CAN has been unique so far, hinders generalization testing to equivalent multimodal datasets from other sites based on alternative scanning methodologies, protocols and devices (Engemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study due to lack of comparable datasets.

claim: The majority of data points is needed for model-fitting and metrics derived from left-out cross-validation splits lack statistical independence.
source: This also renders computation of numerical hypothesis tests (including p-values) more difficult in the context of predictive modeling: The majority of data points is needed for model-fitting and metrics derived from left-out cross-validation splits, for example, predictions of brain age, lack statistical independence.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical limitations in the context of cross-validation.

claim: Procedures optimizing prediction performance in high dimensions are not yet supported by the in-depth understanding required to guarantee formal statistical inferences.
source: Procedures optimizing prediction performance in high dimensions are not yet supported by the in-depth understanding required to guarantee formal statistical inferences, whereas models with well-established procedures for statistical inference lack predictive capability (Bzdok et al., 2018; Bzdok and Ioannidis, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the trade-off between prediction and inference with references to previous literature.

claim: The MEG-features used in the present study were non-exhaustive.
source: Third, the MEG-features used in the present study were non-exhaustive.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Feature-engineering was based on aging-specific literature review constrained by biophysical considerations.
source: Instead, feature-engineering was based on our aging-specific literature review constrained by biophysical considerations.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used.

claim: Non-stationary analyses focusing on transient electrophysiological events may uncover clinically relevant information on cognitive brain dynamics.
source: Recent findings suggest that non-stationary analyses focusing on transient electrophysiological events may uncover clinically relevant information on cognitive brain dynamics (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Baker et al., 2014; Vidaurre et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: MEG and EEG share the same types of neural generators, but their specific biophysics render these methods complementary for studying neuronal activity.
source: Finally, while MEG and EEG share the same types of neural generators, their specific biophysics render these methods complementary for studying neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between MEG and EEG.

claim: There is no public dataset equivalent of the Cam-CAN including EEG or both EEG and MEG.
source: At this point, unfortunately, there is no public dataset equivalent of the Cam-CAN including EEG or, both, EEG and MEG.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of available datasets.
